title: Preparing names in more than one script
description: Text in more than one script needs an exact source and a competent reader.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Text in more than one script needs an exact source and a competent reader. A visual resemblance is not enough to verify characters or meaning.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Provide each language as selectable text where possible and label it clearly. Keep pronunciation notes separate from the exact inscription. Ask a fluent reader to check spelling, character order and intended meaning. Review the actual proposed layout as a separate step.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A name transliterated into another script may have more than one accepted form. Supply the preferred spelling instead of asking the atelier to guess from an English version.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Has a fluent reader checked it?
Which exact version should appear on the object?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: This article does not certify a translation or promise support for every script. Feasibility and the final proof need discussion.

title: A date-format checklist for personalized art
description: Date formats can be ambiguous even when every digit is correct.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Date formats can be ambiguous even when every digit is correct. Write the intended date in words alongside the requested display format.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Record the full date, the preferred visible format and whether separators or month names matter. Keep the occasion date separate from any requested delivery date. Review the final proof character by character. Ask another reader to interpret the displayed date without prompting.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A numeric date such as 04/05 can be read in different orders. Writing the month in words in the brief removes that ambiguity while leaving the visual format open.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Does the display format match the intention?
Are occasion and delivery dates clearly separate?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: An occasion date is not a confirmed production or delivery commitment. Timing requires separate agreement.

title: Checking line breaks before approving text
description: Line breaks change how a short inscription is read.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Line breaks change how a short inscription is read. Showing the intended grouping is more reliable than hoping a layout preserves it automatically.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Provide the complete text first, then a version with preferred line breaks. Mark which breaks are essential and which are flexible. Check punctuation and spacing after copying between applications. Review the final proposed layout rather than only the original message.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A two-line dedication may keep a name together on one line. If the available space changes, the proof needs another reading rather than an automatic smaller type size.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Has the final proof been read in its actual layout?

paragraphs: A preferred layout does not confirm legibility or fabrication feasibility. Those depend on the actual proposal.

title: Choosing a short message that fits its purpose
description: A short message works best when its purpose is clear.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A short message works best when its purpose is clear. Decide whether it identifies, commemorates or expresses a personal sentiment before editing its length.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Write the full intended meaning privately, then choose the words that need to appear on the object. Remove details that belong in a card or private note instead. Check tone with the person responsible for the wording. Keep the approved text separate from alternative drafts.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A brief dedication may carry the intended sentiment more clearly than a compressed paragraph filled with abbreviations. The right length depends on the proposed design.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which wording is the approved source?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not assume a shorter message automatically fits or remains legible. Review the actual proof and confirm feasibility.

title: Organising individual names for a gift set
description: A gift set with individual names needs a structured list.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A gift set with individual names needs a structured list. Repeated copying between messages makes it easier for a name to attach to the wrong item.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Give each intended item a reference and one exact text field. Keep shared wording in a separate section. Identify the source of each spelling and whether it has been checked. Review the list in the same order as the proposed set.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: If every item shares a date but has a different name, state the shared date once and use a clear item-to-name table. Do not infer missing names from previous entries.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Does every item have one reference?
Who has checked each individual spelling?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: The list is a request, not confirmation of quantity, availability, pricing or timing.

title: Sharing a gift reference without revealing private recipient details
description: A gift reference can communicate style without exposing the recipient's address or personal history.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A gift reference can communicate style without exposing the recipient's address or personal history. Share only the details necessary for the current design discussion.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Separate the visual brief from delivery information. Remove identifying background details from reference images where possible. Explain the occasion broadly unless a specific detail affects the design. Keep any intended public story subject to separate permission.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A preference for a quiet blue accent can be discussed without naming the recipient's workplace or sharing a private photograph of their home.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What does the design need to know?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not assume that sending a gift brief authorizes public use of recipient information. Delivery details belong in the appropriate private arrangement.

title: Recording a preferred spelling and pronunciation separately
description: Spelling and pronunciation serve different purposes.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Spelling and pronunciation serve different purposes. Keeping them separate prevents a helpful phonetic note from becoming the inscription itself.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Provide the exact written name in a clearly labelled field. Add pronunciation in a separate note only if useful. Identify capitalization, spacing and punctuation preferences. Ask the responsible person to verify the final proof against the exact text source.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A pronunciation guide may contain hyphens or syllable breaks that should never appear on the object. Labelling it clearly avoids that confusion.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which is only a pronunciation aid?
Has the proof been compared to the source?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: The atelier should not be expected to infer an approved spelling from pronunciation alone. Script support and layout remain subject to discussion.

title: A variation matrix for shared and individual gift details
description: A variation matrix explains which parts of a gift set repeat and which change.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A variation matrix explains which parts of a gift set repeat and which change. This is clearer than several almost identical briefs.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Use rows for items and columns for shared design, individual text and optional differences. Mark blanks as “not requested” or “to confirm” rather than leaving their meaning unclear. Review the matrix for accidental inconsistencies. Link each variation to its own proof when available.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A set may share a colour direction while each item carries different initials. The matrix makes the intended repetition and variation visible together.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A matrix does not establish production feasibility, quantity discounts or a delivery promise. Those need separate agreement.

title: Keeping occasion information separate from delivery commitments
description: An occasion date explains why timing matters, but it does not reserve a production slot.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: An occasion date explains why timing matters, but it does not reserve a production slot. A useful brief distinguishes the event from the request for delivery.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Record the occasion date, preferred arrival period and any flexibility. Explain whether the date is essential or a preference. Ask for feasibility and timing confirmation before making plans dependent on the piece. Keep later agreed dates in the current order discussion.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A gift intended for a celebration may still be meaningful if delivered later, or the timing may be essential. State that distinction instead of assuming it.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which timing has actually been agreed?

title: Proofreading a personalization request with a second reader
description: A second reader can catch errors that become invisible after repeated editing.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A second reader can catch errors that become invisible after repeated editing. Give that reader the exact source and the final proposed proof, not just a description of what it should say.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Ask them to compare names, dates, punctuation, line breaks and script direction. Have them read unfamiliar numeric dates aloud in words. Record any correction against the current version. Repeat the comparison if the proof changes.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A spelling may be correct in the original brief but altered during a later layout revision. The final comparison must therefore use the actual current proof.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Did any later change require another review?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A second reading is a check, not evidence of professional translation or native-reader approval unless the actual qualified reviewer is identified.
